Royal Caribbean late Sunday said the 5,400-passenger Allure of the Seas — one of the world's three biggest cruise ships — would skip a call Thursday in St. Kitts to avoid the storm.

St. Kitts only was added to Allure's itinerary a few days ago as a replacement port for Irma-ravaged St. Maarten — the Dutch side of the island of St. Martin.

More: St. Thomas, St. Martin off Royal Caribbean schedule for weeks | Grand Turk not quite ready for ships | Irma showed up, and this cruise went to the dogs

Allure now will head to Falmouth, Jamaica instead, Royal Caribbean said.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

Also on the move to avoid Maria is Royal Caribbean's Puerto Rico-based Adventure of the Seas, which is heading for Aruba and Bonaire instead of planned stops in Antigua, St. Lucia and Barbados.

Carnival late Sunday announced that itineraries for three vessels already modified due to Irma would again be changing due to Maria.

The 2,974-passenger Carnival Glory, which departed Miami on Saturday, now is heading to the Western Caribbean instead of The Bahamas, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic. It's the third change to the ship's itinerary since the middle of last week. Glory originally was scheduled to visit Half Moon Cay in The Bahamas; St. Thomas; San Juan, Puerto Rico; and Grand Turk Island. On Thursday, the call at St. Thomas was dropped; on Friday the line replaced Grand Turk with Amber Cove in the Dominican Republic.

Also making a last-minute switch to the Western Caribbean from the Eastern Caribbean is the 3,690-passenger Carnival Magic. The Port Canaveral, Fla.-based vessel also has seen multiple changes to its itinerary in recent days.

A third Carnival ship, the 2,056-passenger, San Juan-based Carnival Fascination, now will operate a cruise to Grenada, Barbados, St. Lucia, Antigua and St. Kitts. Its original itinerary called for stops in St. Thomas and St. Maarten.

More: Royal Caribbean begins pulling Key West from itineraries | Royal Caribbean expands commitment to relief effort | St. Thomas off cruise schedules for weeks

Both St. Thomas and St. Martin were devastated by Irma, which barreled across the islands as a Category 5 hurricane. Some officials have hinted it could be many months before they are ready to receive tourists. In an interview with NPR on Wednesday, the governor of the U.S. Virgin Islands said he hoped St. Thomas could be back up and running for tourism by January.

In addition to St. Thomas and St. Martin, cruise ship destinations significantly affected by Irma include Key West, Fla.; St. John in the U.S. Virgin Islands; Barbuda; St. Barts; and Tortola in the British Virgin Islands.

As of 8:00 a.m. ET, Maria was 85 miles east of Martinique and moving to the west-northwest at 12 miles per hour. The storm had maximum sustained winds of 110 miles per hour.

The National Hurricane Center on Monday said Maria is likely to strengthen significantly, and is expected to be at major hurricane intensity when it affects portions of the Leeward Islands over the next few days. It is likely to bring dangerous wind, storm surge and rainfall hazards to the region, the agency said.

The National Hurricane Center also said Maria is likely to affect the British and U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico by mid-week as a dangerous major hurricane.

search_result.title: Tesla unveils Cybercab driverless model in 'We, Robot' event
search_result.text:
Oct. 10, 2024 Updated Oct. 11, 2024, 9:13 a.m. ET

Tesla unveiled a self-driving taxi during the electric car giant's "We, Robot" event Thursday night, paving the path for what CEO Elon Musk has bet will drive long-term growth for the electric vehicle maker.

The two-door models unveiled on the Warner Brothers lot in Burbank, California, had no steering wheels or gas and brake pedals and Musk promised the fully autonomous cars would be, "10 times safer than a human."

The much-hyped event saw 20 so-called Cybercabs and 30 autonomous Model Y cars. Musk said that he expected to begin fully unsupervised self-driving in California and Texas "next year" and that production for the Cybercab would begin in 2026, with the vehicles available for purchase for less than $30,000.

Tesla also revealed a Robovan and that it has made progress on the Optimus personal robot.

Musk pitched the autonomous technology as a way to reduce the need for parking in cities and as a way for drivers to reclaim their time.

The Cybercab was originally slated to be revealed in August but has been publicly touted by Musk since 2019. The announcement comes a week after Reuters reported on Musk's plans to create a Tesla-run autonomous ride service using vehicles owned by his customers when they are not otherwise in use.

Musk wanted to release robotaxis in 2020

In April 2019, Musk revealed that he expected Tesla robotaxis to be fully operating by 2020. The company predicted that each driverless vehicle would withstand 11 years and 1 million miles, earning Tesla $30,000 in annual profit.

Musk also shared that the cars would be accompanied by a ride-share app similar to both Uber and Airbnb. U.S. and Chinese regulators have currently only approved self-driving cars in limited and experimental instances on public roads.

The automotive company faces lawsuits and investigations related to crashes with its existing autopilot and Full Self-Driving driver-assistance systems, which the company has explained were the result of inattentive drivers.

Tesla missed delivery expectations

Tesla missed Wall Street's expectations when it released its third-quarter delivery report last week.

Elecktrek reported that the analyst consensus landed at 463,000 deliveries for the quarter while Tesla reported 462,890.

Model 3 and Model Y made up the vast majority of the deliveries with nearly 440,000 of the two models delivered in the quarter. Tesla delivered just under 23,000 of all other models combined.

(This story has been updated with new information.)

Contributing: Reuters

search_result.title: From Elvis to GloRilla, how Memphis has shaped music in America
search_result.text:
May 20, 2026, 6:03 a.m. ET

As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of the United States, it’s also an opportunity to reflect on Memphis' part in that story. Perhaps no city — and certainly no city of its size — has made as much of an impact on American music and culture as Memphis.

Memphis has been many things: the birthplace of the blues, ground zero for the revolution of rock 'n' roll, and the city that perfected soul. It’s given the world the Father of the Blues, the King of the Blues and the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll, saw the bright light of Sun Records, the soulful sounds of Stax Records and Hi Records, the hitmaking machine of American Sound Studios, helped define Southern Rap and so much more.

In short, the Bluff City has produced more iconic musical figures, more significant records and more zeitgeist-shifting movements than should be possible. Here’s a look at just some of the Memphis artists, producers, labels and scenes that have helped soundtrack the American experience.

W.C. Handy: The Father of the Blues

The self-declared “Father of the Blues,” W.C. Handy was a Beale Street fixture at the turn of the 20th century who would become synonymous with the music of the region. Born in Florence, Alabama, he arrived in Memphis as an itinerant band leader in 1909, quickly raided other local Beale outfits for their best musicians and soon had the top group in town.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

He would ultimately be recognized for what is most often credited as the first published blues song, "The Memphis Blues." As the city's first international star, Handy would transform the blues from a mostly regional folk style into a genre all its own, reshaping popular music in the process with songs like ‘St. Louis Blues,” “Yellow Dog Blues,” “Careless Love” and many others.

As his induction into the Memphis Music Hall of Fame noted, “Handy’s songs had helped create an entire blues industry. Every label was recording blues songs, not just by white vaudevillians like Al Jolson, Emmet Miller and Sophie Tucker, but by such African-American icons as Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, Blind Lemon Jefferson, Papa Charlie Jackson, Blind Blake and more.”

He would later move to New York, where he found major success as a song publisher and traveled the world performing. Handy would have a profound influence on the French composer Maurice Ravel who saw him perform in Paris in the 1920s, and would draw on Handy’s work for his masterpiece, "Sonata for Violin and Piano," which incorporated elements of the blues.

A sharp businessman, an analytically minded student of the music and an important educational figure and author, Handy died in 1958, but his impact as a seminal figure in the history of the blues — one of America’s greatest art forms — continues on.

B.B. King: The King of the Blues

He was, to all who ever heard him play, the one true king of the blues. A musical giant, cultural icon and pre-eminent influence on guitarists for more than 60 years, B.B. King was singularly synonymous with the genre he loved and helped turn it into a global touchstone. King was lavished with praise for more than half a century by his fellow artists, with several generations of the world’s biggest musical stars citing his emotive singing, lyrical playing and unparalleled vibrato as the height of the blues and the foundation of their own work.

Born Riley B. King in Berclair, Mississippi, in 1925, by the late ’40s King had moved to the Bluff City, where he soaked up the hothouse musical atmosphere. Before long, King went knocking on the doors of Memphis’ newly launched all-Black-operated radio station WDIA. After a successful audition in the lobby of the station, he landed a daily 15-minute spot as “The Pepticon Boy” — selling the booze-filled “health tonic.” King — who picked up the moniker Blues Boy, and finally, B.B. — would rise through the regional entertainment ranks, playing both deep and urbane blues on “Lucille,” the nickname given to his Gibson guitar. He began recording at Sam Phillips’ fledgling Memphis Recording Service, releasing his first sides for the Modern and R.P.M. labels.

In 1952, he scored his first hit record, the chart-topping R&B number “3 O’Clock Blues.” Over the next decade, he would release a steady stream of hit singles, helping him rise from the Chitlin’ Circuit to the pinnacle of Black entertainment. His crack big band show, as captured on a 1964 album recorded in Chicago, "Live at the Regal," remains one of the great blues albums. King’s work would resonate especially strongly in Britain, where a generation of budding blues guitarists — from Eric Clapton to Jeff Beck to Jimmy Page — would feel his impact in the 1960s. King’s influence on this generation of rockers would lead to his late ’60s/early ’70s crossover to the white market. He would have his biggest chart triumph with 1969’s Top 20 hit and Grammy-winning single, “The Thrill Is Gone.”

By the ’70s, King had become a sort of ambassador for the blues, exposing the music to its biggest audiences through his performances on Ed Sullivan and Johnny Carson’s “Tonight Show.” King continued to tour tirelessly over the next few decades, spending an average of 250 nights on the road. He opened stadium shows for the likes of the Rolling Stones and U2, made appearances in a dozen films, headlined festivals and released more than 80 albums. He died in 2015 but his legacy continues through the B.B. King Museum and Delta Interpretive Center in his hometown or Indianola, Mississippi.

Sam Phillips and Sun Records

The brainchild of visionary producer Sam Phillips, Sun Records and its artists would quite literally shape the musical world and have an unmistakable impact on American culture.

Born in Florence, Alabama (hometown of that other Memphis music master, W.C. Handy), Phillips and Sun "created the most crucial, uplifting, and powerful records ever made," as Bob Dylan wrote in his memoir, "Chronicles."

The youngest son of a farming clan, Phillips would be shaped by many forces, none more so than an almost fanatical belief in the importance of individualism. As his biographer Peter Guralnick noted, Phillips felt "the implied responsibility — no, the obligation — for each of us to be as different as our individuated natures allowed us to be. To be different, in Sam's words, to the extreme."

Phillips would discover and record just those kinds of artists, some the most distinctive voices of their or any other era. He gave them opportunity and animation and thrust them into a world that would be forever changed by their songs and sounds.

After spending his early years in radio, in January 1950 Phillips opened the Memphis Recording Service at 706 Union Ave. For the first couple years, Phillips recorded mostly blues acts for outside labels like Chess, R.P.M. and Modern, while doing custom recordings of weddings and funerals in between.

In early 1953, Phillips put out the first release on his newly launched Sun Records label: “Drivin' Slow,” an instrumental by teenage saxophonist Johnny London. The song would be the modest starting point in a remarkable odyssey for Phillips and his company, which would go onto launch the careers of Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, Roy Orbison and Carl Perkins, among others.

After his success with Sun in the 1950s, Phillips built a new studio, the Sam Phillips Recording Service. He eventually sold the Sun label in 1969 to Nashville producer and music biz impresario Shelby Singleton. After purchasing the company from Phillips, Singleton formed the Sun Entertainment Corporation, which controlled the Sun music and logo for the next 52 years (though the Phillips family would continue to maintain a small interest in the company). In 2021 Singleton’s family sold the Sun holdings — for an undisclosed price, though estimated to be around $30 million — to music rights company Primary Wave.

Elvis Presley: The King of Rock 'n' Roll

As with other seminal Memphis music figures like Handy and King, you would be hard pressed to overstate the importance of Elvis Aaron Presley.

Inducted into the inaugural class of the Rock ‘n’ Roll Hall of Fame, Presley was hailed for igniting “a musical — and cultural — revolution with his firebrand take on blues, country, R&B, pop, bluegrass, and gospel.” More than that, Presley brought Black-based music to a mass mainstream white audience and thus began a cultural cross-pollination that would forever reshape popular music. Galvanizing teen audiences in new and unprecedented ways, his career would establish the blueprint for a new kind of global star and pop phenomenon.

Presley’s success — as a recording artist, film star and touring performer — remains largely unmatched. According to Elvis’ official website, it's estimated that more than 1 billion Elvis records have been sold worldwide, more than anyone in history. Presley has some 150 albums and singles that have been certified gold, platinum or multi-platinum. And he has scored 114 top 40 hits, 40 in the top 10, and 18 No. 1s.

His groundbreaking television appearances in the 1950s on Ed Sullivan would electrify and shock audiences, his long movie career would see him star in more than 30 pictures and make him one of Hollywood’s top box office draws, while his touring work in the 1950s and again in the 1970s would become legendary.

His influence on almost every artist and genre that came after him is undeniable. From Buddy Holly to the Beatles, David Bowie to Bruce Springsteen, Lana Del Rey to Post Malone, Presley's impact has been felt continuously across the last eight decades.

ELVIS PRESLEY IN HIS OWN WORDS: The King on music, movies, Memphis and more

Stax, Hi and Memphis Soul

Located just a short distance from each other in South Memphis, Stax Records and Hi Records would become the twin giants of American soul music.

In 1957, a full-time banker and part-time fiddler by the name of Jim Stewart started a little homespun record company called Satellite, cutting local country and rockabilly acts. A few years later, joined by a new partner in his sister Estelle Axton, they would move operations to an old movie theater on McLemore Avenue in South Memphis. In the process the company would be recast as an R&B label, which would eventually evolve into one of the paragons of soul music, known the world over: Stax Records.

Stewart and Axton would tap the talents of a core of young South Memphis neighborhood kids to make its records: Booker T. Jones, William Bell, David Porter and Isaac Hayes, among them. A remarkable contingent of artists — from Otis Redding to Sam & Dave and The Staple Singers — would come to define the Stax sound, as the company, later led by former disc jockey Al Bell, became a soul institution through the 1960s until its demise in 1975.

At roughly the same time, Royal Studios, the historic home of Hi Records, was becoming the playhouse of Al Green and Ann Peebles, the laboratory of the estimable Hi Rhythm house band and a product of the unwavering vision of their producer and guiding light, Willie Mitchell.

Hi Records was founded in 1957 by a group of partners that included former Sun Rockabilly artist Ray Harris, and two other Sun alumni, Bill Cantrell and Quinton Claunch. Local record store-owner and jukebox merchant Joe Cuoghi provided further financial backing. Hi was headquartered out of an old movie theater on South Lauderdale, built in 1915, that had been turned into a recording studio, called Royal.

Though the company would initially become identified with hit instrumental records from the likes Elvis’ former bassist Bill Black’s Combo and saxophonist Ace Cannon, it was R&B band leader and producer Mitchell who would come to define the sound of Royal and Hi. Starting in the late-'60s, Mitchell took over the label and studio operation and over the next decade he'd help reshape the history of soul music with hits for Green, Peebles, Otis Clay and others, while establishing his handpicked Hi Rhythm Section as one of the great house bands of all time.

Since Mitchell's death in 2013, the studio has been run by his family, with the production side handled by his son Lawrence "Boo" Mitchell. The younger Mitchell has carried on the tradition admirably, earning Grammy Awards for his work on a number of high-profile projects including the Bruno Mars/Mark Ronson hit "Uptown Funk." He's also re-established the studio as a sought-after workspace, with Keith Richards and the Wu-Tang Clan, Robert Plant and Paul Rodgers among the many acts who've made pilgrimages to Royal to record in recent years.

Chips Moman and American Sound Studios

Born in Georgia in 1937, Lincoln "Chips" Moman hitchhiked to Memphis at age 17, where he was discovered by Sun Records star Warren Smith. Moman later joined up with brothers Johnny and Dorsey Burnette, traveling with them for sessions in California at the famed Gold Star Recording Studios, where learned the craft of recording and producing.

His chance to fulfill his own destiny behind the board came when he was called to do a session at a tiny garage studio in Brunswick, Tennessee, owned by Jim Stewart. Moman and Stewart hit it off and decided to join forces to start what would become Satellite, and eventually Stax Records.

Moman played a pivotal role in Stax's development. He was the one who recorded the label's initial hits by Carla Thomas, Rufus Thomas and William Bell; helped develop "Last Night," the song that would become The Mar-Keys' smash; and was the one who was musically predisposed to turning Stax from a white country music company into a Black R&B label in the first place. But a rancorous split in 1962 with Stewart and his sister and co-owner, Estelle Axton, brought all that to an abrupt end.

In 1965, Moman began developing a studio at 827 N. Thomas. American Sound Studios took off with the arrival of local teen garage band The Gentrys, who cut a million-selling smash called "Keep on Dancing."

American Studios would become a veritable hit factory that produced more than 120 chart records during its peak years. With Moman guiding them, the American house band, later known as the Memphis Boys — guitarist Reggie Young, drummer Gene Chrisman, pianist Bobby Wood, organist Bobby Emmons and bassists Mike Leech and Tommy Cogbill — would provide the essential ballast and delicate filigree found in the hits of Dusty Springfield ("Son of a Preacher Man"), Neil Diamond ("Sweet Caroline"), Merrilee Rush ("Angel of the Morning"), B.J. Thomas ("Hooked on a Feeling"), Joe Tex ("I Gotcha"), Bobby Womack ("Fly Me To The Moon") and, perhaps most famously, Elvis Presley ("Suspicious Minds").

Moman left Memphis in 1972 and headed to Atlanta to start a new studio, taking most of the American band with him. His tenure in Atlanta was short-lived, however. After encountering problems with the new record label he'd set up, Moman decided to get out of the music business entirely.

Instead, he stopped in Nashville and wrote a hit song for B.J. Thomas ("(Hey Won't You Play) Another Somebody Done Somebody Wrong Song"), and decided to continue in Music City. Moman would spend the next dozen years in Nashville, where he would dominate the country field — writing hits and producing albums by Willie Nelson, Waylon Jennings, Tammy Wynette and Ronnie Milsap.

Moman made a brief, ill-fated return to Memphis recording in the mid-‘80s. Long overlooked for his contributions, in the summer of 2014, Moman and company were finally given some overdue recognition in the Bluff City. A Shelby County historical marker was placed on the site where American Studios once stood. Moman was also inducted into the Memphis Music Hall of Fame that year.

Memphis Rap: Underground origins and influencers

Like all musical forms, no one person can definitively say they started or invented Memphis rap, though there are plenty of seminal figures who were crucial in the development of the genre, from DJ Spanish Fly to DJ Squeeky, Gangsta Pat to Playa Fly, Al Kapone to Tommy Wright III. But arguably two acts loom largest, in terms of reputation and influence, on the whole of Memphis rap: Three 6 Mafia and 8Ball & MJG.

Formed in 1991 — by DJ Paul, Lord Infamous and Juicy J — Three 6 Mafia put out nine full-length LPs (as well as myriad mixtapes, collaborations and side projects) during their initial 21-year run, during which they helped define the sound of the Dirty South.

The group — which has sold more than 5 million albums — hit the charts in the mid-2000s, with singles "Stay Fly" and "Poppin' My Collar," off their "Most Known Unknown" LP. Released in 2005, the disc would become the band's biggest seller, reaching No. 3 on the Billboard pop charts, a portent of even bigger things to come.

In 2006 — 34 years after Stax legend Isaac Hayes earned an Oscar in the same category for "Theme from Shaft" — Three 6 Mafia won the Academy Award for Best Original Song. The group nabbed the trophy for "It's Hard Out Here for a Pimp" — co-written by Hypnotize Minds artist Frayser Boy — their contribution to writer-director Craig Brewer's made-in-Memphis "Hustle & Flow." The group's performance on the Oscar telecast and their unexpected win suddenly made them household names.

The band would eventually follow with the 2008 album "Last 2 Walk" (another top five-charting LP), their own MTV reality show "Adventures in Hollyhood," and plans for a series of Three 6-branded films and other multimedia content. Though the group would splinter, with its members going on to various solo pursuits, Three 6’s legacy was confirmed when it was inducted into the Memphis Music Hall of Fame, as part of its inaugural class in 2012.

Along with Three 6 Mafia, the dominating duo of 8Ball & MJG certainly have had the deepest and most profound impact on Bluff City hip-hop. Marlon Jermaine Goodwin and Premro "8Ball" Smith were raised in Orange Mound and met while being bused to Ridgeway Middle School in the mid-‘80s. Forming an instant bond over their shared loved of the then still-fledgling art of hip-hop, the two developed their signature style, which debuted to the world — or at least the underground — with 1991’s “Listen to the Lyrics.”

Their proper run of studio LPs in the ‘90s began with the 1993 classic “Comin Out Hard” and continued with the following year’s “On the Outside Looking In,” before the group went gold and hit the Billboard charts with 1995’s “On Top of the World.” In between separate solo projects, the pair ended the ‘90s with another gold seller in 1999’s hip-hop album chart topper “In Our Lifetime.”

Having helped make Southern rap a viable — both creatively and commercially — alternative to the West and East Coast scenes, 8Ball & MJG entered the 2000s by signing a deal with P. Diddy's Bad Boy record label. Their 2004 Bad Boy debut “Living Legends” took the group to new heights, landing the pair at the top of the rap chart and at No. 3 on the album chart.

Their 2005 collaboration with Three 6 Mafia on the double platinum “Stay Fly” would mark a kind of zenith for these progenitors of Memphis rap. The pair has continued to flourish, leading their own record labels, reuniting to sign to T.I.’s Grand Hustle label and releasing “Ten Toes Down” in 2010. 8Ball & MJG would follow Three 6 Mafia into the Memphis Music Hall of Fame in 2018, making them the second hip-hop inductees.

Memphis Rap: Mainstream stars

While Memphis rap's underground forefathers would have a profound influence on the genre, it would be a newer generation of rappers who would take Memphis rap to mainstream success and the top of the Billboard charts.

The 2000s' flowering of Memphis rap was led by the veteran MC and label owner Yo Gotti. In addition to his own breakout success in 2014, after years of underground fame, Gotti would help bring the talents of artists like Moneybagg Yo and GloRilla to the world via his CMG record label.

The career of Moneybagg Yo began to take flight in 2019, with the release of his second full-length project, "43va Heartless," which debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard chart. A year later he broke through on an even bigger scale with the album "Time Served." Released in early 2020, the record — a star-studded project featuring collaborations with Future, Da Baby, Lil Baby, Megan Thee Stallion, Summer Walker and Fredo Bang — hit No. 3 on the album charts. A deluxe version was also released, and the two projects have collectively been streamed more than 2 billion times globally.

In 2020, Moneybagg followed up with "Code Red", a collaborative project with Blac Youngsta. The two rappers got their start together in local hip-hop group Memphis Greatest Unrated before going on to solo careers. The joint effort also debuted on the Billboard Top 10. But his real breakthrough came with his 2021 album, “A Gangsta’s Pain,” which topped the Billboard charts — twice, in fact. The last Memphis artist to achieve the No. 1 spot was pop superstar Justin Timberlake.

In June 2024, Moneybagg released his much-anticipated follow-up, “Speak Now.” The record found 'Bagg expanding his sound and reach, including a collaboration with country superstar Morgan Wallen (on "Whiskey Whiskey," which became a rap chart hit) and R&B singer Chris Brown, and the album again became a gold-certified success reaching No. 3 on the hip-hop charts and No. 13 on the pop charts.

Even as Moneybagg grew his fame, another Memphis artist, GloRilla, was rising quickly representing a new female force in hip-hop. GloRilla began her rap career not quite a decade ago. In late 2018, she put out her first video, “146 Freestyle,” and followed with a pair of indie EPs, "Most Likely Up Next" in 2019 and “P Status” in 2020. Eventually, in spring 2021, she caught the attention of top Memphis producer HitKidd who teamed GloRilla with a group of other emerging female rappers for an EP called “Set the Tone.”

She would embark on a solo career in 2022, releasing the EP “Anyway, Life’s Great," featuring the single “F.N.F. (Let’s Go)” — another collaboration with HitKidd — which became a viral hit then a chart success, getting her signed to Gotti’s CMG label that year.

Her debut album, “Glorious,” was released in 2023 and hit No. 5 on the Billboard album charts and made it to No. 2 on the R&B/Hip-Hop charts. In 2024, she had five songs chart on the Billboard Hot 100: "Wanna Be" with Megan Thee Stallion at No. 11, "Whatchu Kno About Me" with Sexyy Red at No. 17, "TGIF" at No. 22, "Yeah Glo!" at No. 28 and "Hollon" at No. 48.

In 2024, GloRilla ascended to full-blown celebrity, as she visited the White House and then-President Joe Biden, was a featured performer at the MTV Video Music Awards, earned a pair of Grammy nominations for Best Rap Song and Best Rap Performance, made the best album and song of the year lists from Rolling Stone magazine, was named one of the Associated Press’ “Breakthrough Entertainers,” and appeared as the musical guest on NBC’s “Saturday Night Live.”

Now a six-time Grammy nominee, GloRilla is expected to release one of 2026’s most anticipated albums as she continues to make her case as one of Memphis' biggest modern musical stars.

search_result.title: 250 Memphis artists and entertainers who have left a lasting mark
search_result.text:
Aug. 2, 2026, 10:48 p.m. ET

As you know, the United States of America this year is celebrating its 250th birthday.

Also as you know, Memphis, Tennessee, is a city within those united states.

So, in recognition of the country's semiquincentennial, here's a proudly Memphicentric and crazily ambitious if inevitably incomplete list of 250 — count 'em, *250* — Memphis artists and entertainers.

Presented in alphabetical order, these are men and women (and waterfowl) who have earned recognition or attracted attention or made a significant contribution to national and even world culture through literature, art, music, theater, film, television, professional wrestling and other forms of art and entertainment, outside of sports.

In other words, you won't find political boss E.H. Crump or Tiger basketball great Larry Finch or serial killer George Howard Putt here. Nor will you find arts-and-entertainment celebrities whose fame is pretty much confined to the Mid-South, such as local television personalities and radio deejays. Rather, this list primarily is devoted to "creatives" with broader appeal or celebrity.

Of course, concocting such a list is a fraught and problematic endeavor. Who to put in, who to leave out? We tried to compile a diverse lineup. We tried not to overemphasize Memphis music or to rely too heavily on Sun or Stax or hip-hop; but notable Memphis musicians alone number way beyond 250, so, yes, music dominates. Even so, some readers will search in vain for a favorite singer or rapper.

In addition, we tried to focus on true Memphians or people who spent a good deal of time here when making their art; but we made allowance for such anchor babies of the arts as Aretha Franklin, who was born here but soon skedaddled. As with the Fourteenth Amendment, being born here is good enough.

And, despite the numerals, this is in no way a "Top 250," even though it includes such undeniable heavy-hitters as Elvis, Isaac and Eggleston, and it's not definitive. It's a sample. It could continue with an additional 250 names, with ease, and then more and more after that. What it is, is this: a list to read, enjoy and debate.

MEMPHIS MUSIC HISTORY: From Elvis to GloRilla, how Memphis has shaped music in America

1. Johnny Ace (1929-1954)

Immortalized in song by Paul Simon as "The Late Great Johnny Ace," this R&B balladeer known for the 1954 hit "Pledging My Love" and for his association with the loose affiliation of top musicians known as "The Beale Streeters" died at age 25 when he shot himself in the head while playing with a pistol.

2. Ilunga Adell

This Hamilton High School graduate was a New York playwright when producers — sensitive to criticism that their Black-themed sitcom did not have enough Black writers — recruited him to pen screenplays for NBC's hit "Sanford and Son." In the career that followed, he wrote for "That's My Mama," "227," "Married... with Children" and "Moesha."

3. Kentucker Audley

Memphis’ contributor to the lo-fi regional filmmaking “mumblecore” movement, the still active actor/director and founder of the streaming platform NoBudge worked alongside such then-indie stalwarts as Greta Gerwig and Lena Dunham, and collaborated in Memphis with such D.I.Y. auteurs as Joe Swanberg and David Lowery.

4. Estelle Axton (1918-2004)

With her brother Jim Stewart, she founded Stax (the name is a combination of Stewart and Axton), the label and studio that made Memphis a hit-making capitol of rhythm-and-blues and soul music in the 1960s and '70s.

5. Harmon E. Baker (1887-1993)

Achieving late-in-life fame as perhaps the nation's oldest practicing professional magician, the 5-foot-1 "Baffling Mr. Baker" was 96 when he traded tricks with Johnny Carson on "The Tonight Show" and 102 when he brought David Letterman to his knees with his "Chinese Death Grip." He died at age 106.

6. Julien Baker

Through her often heartrending solo work and her collaborations with Phoebe Bridgers and Lucy Dacus in the indie "supergroup" boygenius, this singer-songwriter from suburban Memphis (Germantown/Bartlett/Arlington) has earned Grammy awards, critical hosannas and a passionate and loyal following with bravely honest songs that examine Christianity, sexuality and mental anxiety.

7. The Bar-Kays

The Stax studio band known for the explosive “Soul Finger” lost most of its original members in the Otis Redding plane crash, then reincarnated as dance-floor-filling funketeers in the 1970s, with such hits as “Shake Your Rump to the Funk” and “Sexomatic.”

8. Kathy Bates

She earned a diploma from White Station High School in 1966 and a Best Actress Oscar for "Misery" in 1991.

9. Michael Beck

Known as Michael Beck Taylor when he played football at Memphis University School, the Memphis-born actor shortened his name for his major movie debut: the lead role of Swan in Walter Hill's stylized and then-controversial (it reportedly inspired real-life violence) gang epic, "The Warriors" (1979). Beck next romanced a supernatural Olivia Newton-John in "Xanadu" (1980).

10. Al Bell

The former Little Rock disc jockey became Stax promotions director in 1965 and then an activist co-owner of the company in 1969, organizing the "Wattstax" event and updating the label’s mission for an era of heavier sounds and heavier thoughts.

11. Chris Bell (1951-1978)

Alongside Alex Chilton, the British Invasion-influenced East Memphis garage rock innovator was the key singer and songwriter in the initially ignored but now revered Memphis power pop band, Big Star. Sensitive and disillusioned, he quit the band after its first album, and was killed in 1978 in an auto accident at age 27, as he was attempting to launch a solo career.

12. William Bell

The Memphis-born soul singer was one of Stax’s most authentic vocalists, breaking hearts with his 1961 breakout single, “You Don't Miss Your Water.”

13. Bill Black (1926-1965)

Elvis Presley’s bass player during the “Big Bang of Rock ‘n' Roll” sessions at Sun, Black found another level of stardom with his instrumental group, Bill Black’s Combo, which opened for the Beatles during the band’s first American tour.

14. The Blackwood Brothers

Multi-generational gospel stars since 1934, the Blackwoods relocated from Mississippi to Memphis in 1950, influencing Elvis Presley, performing with many country artists, and becoming a dominant force in sacred music. (With his brothers or as a solo artist, James Backwood — who died in 2002 at 82 — is reportedly the only artist to have been nominated for a Grammy for 28 successive years.)

15. Bobby 'Blue' Bland (1930-2013)

Based in Germantown in his later years, the "Sinatra of the Blues" began his long career on Beale Street, moaning "They Call It Stormy Monday" with the force of a gathering thunderhead.

16. Scott Bomar

A longtime ubiquitous contributor to the Memphis punk/soul scene (notably as bass player with the ace surf/noir/jazz combo, Impala, and with his retro-soul ensemble, the Bo-Keys), Bomar has founded a studio and a label (Electraphonic), engineered and produced music by Al Green and Cyndi Lauper, and been an essential creative partner with director Craig Brewer, composing scores for such projects as "Hustle & Flow," "Black Snake Moan" and "Song Sung Blue."

17. Stanley Booth (1942-2024)

Perhaps best-known for “The True Adventures of the Rolling Stones,” his 1984 book about touring with the superstar band in the Altamont year of 1969, the hard-living music journalist brought an extremely personal dimension to his portraits of such artists as Elvis Presley, Otis Redding and Gram Parsons.

18. Craig Brewer

Memphis' most accessible major writer-director has led actors to Academy Award nominations (Terrence Howard in "Hustle & Flow," Kate Hudson in "Song Sung Blue"), songwriters to an actual Oscar and Eddie Murphy to a "Coming to America" sequel.

19. W. Herbert Brewster (1897-1987)

The longtime pastor of East Trigg Avenue Baptist Church, Brewster was one of the most significant composers in gospel music, publishing more than 200 songs, including hits for such praise-making giants as the Soul Stirrers, Marion Williams and Mahalia Jackson.

20. Don Bryant (1942-2025)

A crucial songwriter and performer for Memphis' Hi Records in the 1970s, Bryant — who married singer Ann Peebles (see below) in 1974 — received late-in-life recognition after he returned to performing and recording in the decade before his death.

21. Jeff Buckley (1966-1997)

The California-born singer-songwriter with the angel's voice and the Pre-Raphaelite face cemented his legend and legacy to Memphis when he drowned in Wolf River Harbor on May 29, 1997, less than a year after moving here to recharge his life and career.

22. Johnny Burnette (1934-1964)

Dubbed "The Johnny Burnette Trio" on the record's label, Memphis brothers Johnny (vocals) and Dorsey Burnette (bass), plus pal Paul Burlison (lead guitar), electrified listeners in 1956 with their supercharged cover of “Train Kept A-Rolling," which later inspired the Yardbirds and Aerosmith. Transitioning from proto-punk to dreamboat, Johnny had a No. 3 1960 solo hit with "You're Sixteen," a song that went to No. 1 in 1974 when it was covered by Ringo Starr. Johnny drowned at age 30.

23. Cedric Burnside

Born in Memphis and raised in Holly Springs, the guitarist, drummer and grandson of hill country blues legend R.L. Burnside carries on a family legacy that continues to inspire numerous players in the Mid-South, the Mississippi Delta and beyond.

24. Ace Cannon (1934-2018)

The saxophone-playing Tech High School alum scored a series of tersely named instrumental hits — "Tuff," "Drunk" —in the 1960s and '70s.

25. Gus Cannon (1883-1979)

Born on a plantation in Red Banks, Mississippi, this Memphis jug band veteran of the 1920s and ‘30s returned to the spotlight when his 1929 recording “Walk Right In” was revived in 1963, becoming a No. 1 hit for the Rooftop Singers, a Greenwich Village folk group.

26. James Carr (1942-2001)

"The Dark End of the Street” (1967) is the signature song of this gospel-influenced artist whose battles with bipolar disorder seem reflected in his heartrending vocals. No wonder aficionados rank him among history’s greatest soul singers.

27. Dixie Carter (1939-2010)

An actress in Memphis stage productions as a college student, she eventually made it to Broadway and later found fame as Julia Sugarbaker, the outspoken lead character on the Atlanta-set CBS sitcom "Designing Women" (1986-1993).

28. Johnny Cash (1932-2003)

Cutting his first records at Sun, this truth-telling singer-songwriter brought the lanky frame and chiseled face of Abe Lincoln, the gravitas of an Old Testament prophet and the chugging rhythm of a steam locomotive to country music.

29. Rosanne Cash

The acclaimed alt-country singer-songwriter was born in Memphis, the oldest of the four daughters of Johnny Cash and his first wife, Vivian.

30. Barbara Cason (1928-1990)

Active in local television and theater in the 1950s (she was a co-founder of the once prominent Front St. Theatre), the Memphis-born-and-raised Cason had a busy post-Memphis career on Broadway, in the movies (including in such succès cultes as “The Honeymoon Killers” and “Exorcist II: The Heretic”), and on television, where she was Cloris Phebus on the ABC sitcom “Carter Country” and Garry’s mother, Ruth, on “It’s Garry Shandling’s Show.”

31. Ben Cauley (1947-2015)

The sole survivor of the 1967 Otis Redding plane crash, the trumpet player and founding Bar-Kays member made music for almost another four decades.

32. Ellen Chenoweth

Since the early 1980s, this 1964 graduate of White Station High School has been one of Hollywood's busiest and most influential casting directors, working regularly with the Coen Brothers and James L. Brooks, and assembling rosters of current and/or future all-stars for such films as "Diner," "Michael Clayton" and "Eddington."

33. Alex Chilton (1950-2010)

A "blue-eyed soul" teen prodigy when "The Letter" and "Cry Like a Baby" were made-in-Memphis hits for his band, the Box Tops, Chilton abandoned his gruff vocal style to be a reedy singer-songwriter in the influential 1970s Memphis power pop combo, Big Star. Then he rejected stardom in favor of a stubborn and eccentric individualism, musically and otherwise, that made him an icon for the punk and "indie" artists in his wake.

34. William Christenberry (1936-2016)

With deep ties to Memphis (including a lengthy 1960s teaching gig at Memphis State University), this acclaimed Tuscaloosa-born artist became known — like his friend and contemporary, William Eggleston — for color photographs of the South.

35. Quinton Claunch (1921-2021)

As a co-founder of both the Hi and Goldwax record companies, this Tishomingo, Mississippi-born musician was an essential enabler of Memphis soul.

36. Carroll Cloar (1913-1993)

A Memphis resident from 1953 until his death, this painter could merge folksy realism with magic surrealism, presenting sharply detailed images of African American wedding parties, a field swarming with "hostile butterflies," and a goblin-masked child confronted by white-sheeted Halloween ghosts that might be members of the Ku Klux Klan.

37. Olivia Cole (1942-2018)

The Memphis-born actress won an Emmy for her role as Matilda, the wife of Chicken George (Ben Vereen), in the groundbreaking 1977 ABC miniseries about slavery and its aftermath, "Roots."

38. George Coleman

Still active at 91, this Memphis saxophonist played with Miles Davis and Herbie Hancock.

39. Frank Cotham

Since 1993, the prolific Bartlett-based cartoonist has contributed single-panel gags to The New Yorker, connecting Memphis to a storied lineage that includes such giants of pen-and-ink as James Thurber, Charles Addams and William Steig.

40. Hank Crawford (1934-2009)

Among other accomplishments, the saxophonist from Manassas High School was Ray Charles’ bandleader.

41. Steve Cropper (1941-2025)

A Memphis soul MVP: He was co-writer of such classics as “Knock on Wood,” “In the Midnight Hour” and “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay," and his precise, tasty guitar licks made him essential to Booker T. & the MG’s and the Stax sound.

42. Jimmy Crosthwait

With the long hair and mischievous demeanor of a rustic hippy wizard, this washboard-strumming member of the Memphis supergroup Mudboy & the Neutrons was also an experimental puppeteer and a participant in avant-garde “Electric Circus” happenings in New York.

43. Rick Dees

He was the top deejay on the city's hottest radio station, WMPS AM-680, when he cut "Disco Duck" as a lark (avian pun intended) in 1976. Credited to "Rick Dees & His Cast of Idiots" but with all-star local talent in support (the producer was Stax stalwart Bobby Manuel), the disco spoof became an unexpected smash, reaching the top spot on the Billboard charts and selling 6 million copies. Unfortunately, Dees' follow-up novelty tune, "Dis-Gorilla," "pretty much bombed," according to the Memphis Press-Scimitar.

44. Eric Jerome Dickey (1961-2021)

Born and raised in South Memphis, this prolific author attracted millions of readers with erotic thrillers, fraught love stories and sagas of domestic crisis and international intrigue that presented a particularly action-packed version of contemporary Black life. To wit: "Bad Men and Wicked Women," the 24th of his 29 novels, was promoted with this characteristic tagline: "Affairs of the heart can be lethal!"

45. Jim Dickinson (1941-2009)

This North Mississippi-based White Station High School graduate (he sometimes billed himself as "East Memphis Slim") seemed to encompass, within his 50-year career, the entire history of rock 'n' roll, from his recordings for Sun (his band was fittingly named "The Jesters"); to his session work with the Rolling Stones (he plays piano on "Wild Horses") and Bob Dylan; to his role as generations-spanning producer/sage for such making-a-pilgrimage-to-Memphis bands as the Replacements and Green on Red; to his endorsement of "world boogie" (diverse, spirit-freeing and rule-breaking roots music).

46. DJ Paul

Paul Duane Beauregard was just a teen when he joined fellow South Memphis kid Ricky Terrell Dunigan (Lord Infamous) and North Memphis hip-hop prodigy Jordan Houston (Juicy J) to form Three 6 Mafia, the pioneering hardcore Southern rap group. In 2006, Paul, Juicy and Memphis rap artist Frayser Boy (Cedric Coleman) shared the Best Original Song Oscar for "It's Hard Out Here for a Pimp," from the made-in-Memphis "Hustle & Flow."

47. DJ Spanish Fly

Sometimes called “The Godfather of Memphis Rap,” Antonio D. Kimbrough began creating tapes at home in the 1980s, developing a raw, electro-funk vibe that would become a trademark of Southern hip-hop.

MEMPHIS SPORTS STARS TO KNOW: From Parlow to Penny, how Memphis has left its mark on sports in America

48. Shannen Doherty (1971-2024)

The Memphis-born former child star ("Little House on the Prairie") and teen actress ("Heathers") found fame alongside Jason Priestley, Tori Spelling, Luke Perry and other hot young performers in the hit Fox series "Beverly Hills, 90210."

49. Donnie Dunagan

An impoverished Memphis kid, he was spotted by a talent scout and cast as the child of Baron Wolf von Frankenstein (Basil Rathbone) in 1939's "Son of Frankenstein" (Donnie's Southern drawl adds an incongruous element to the Gothic expressionist esthetic). However, his main claim to movie fame came within a less spooky context: Young Donnie provided the voice for the young "Bambi" in the 1942 Disney animated film.

50. Donald 'Duck' Dunn (1941-2012)

The second and longest-lasting bass player in Booker T. & the MG’s (he succeeded Lewie Steinberg), Dunn also was recruited by Dan Aykroyd and John Belushi to join several other Memphis soul alumni in the Blues Brothers band.

51. Mignon Dunn (1928-2026)

The "lusty mezzo from Memphis" (to quote The New York Times) was a star of the famed Metropolitan Opera from the 1950s through the 1990s.

52. William Eggleston

A 1976 exhibition of his pictures — snapshot-style Southern subjects elevated from the mundane to the heroic with saturated color and uncanny composition — at the Museum of Modern Art in New York affirmed the legitimacy of color photography, establishing this scion of Delta privilege as one of Memphis' most influential and startling artists since Elvis.

53. 8Ball & MJG

Friends since their days at Ridgeway Middle School and still going strong, the Orange Mound duo of Premro "8Ball" Smith and Marlon Jermaine "MJG" Goodwin helped tag Memphis as a rap mecca with their mission statement of a debut album, "Comin' Out Hard," in 1993.

54. Chris Ellis

The caricaturist and once frequent Memphis stage presence was known locally for his acerbic deadpan wit but onscreen he mostly has incarnated stolid authority figures, with supporting roles in such blockbusters as "Armageddon," "The Dark Knight Rises" and "Apollo 13."

55. Kallen Esperian

The glamorous Memphis soprano's triumphs include Metropolitan Opera performances alongside such superstars as Luciano Pavarotti and Plácido Domingo and an international tour in the 1990s with divas Kathleen Cassello and Cynthia Lawrence, billed as "The Three Sopranos" (to suggest the famous "Three Tenors" teaming of Pavarotti, Domingo and José Carreras).

56. David Evans

The Boston-born longtime University of Memphis ethnomusicologist founded the school's High Water record label, bringing overdue exposure to such area blues artist as the Fieldstones, Junior Kimbrough and "The She-Wolf," Jessie Mae Hemphill.

57. Tav Falco

The self-invented thaumaturge, dramaturge and demiurge of a peculiarly influential Memphis demimonde of the late 1970s and '80s, the former Gustavo Nelson of Clark County, Arkansas, attracted worldwide albeit mostly underground attention with the "art-damaged" musical "conjurations" of his punk-roots-blues-garage collective, Panther Burns.

58. John Farris

Based on his experiences at Central High School, his provocative 1959 novel, "Harrison High," written while he was a student at Southwestern (now Rhodes College), was a best-seller. But he became better known for horror, with his 1976 novel "The Fury" providing the basis for the Brian De Palma film.

59. Charlie Feathers (1932-1998)

His eccentric hiccup delivery and rustic yet somehow unearthly aura place him in the top tier of rockabilly-country artists, according to the enthusiasts who discovered his music decades after its creation.

60. Ben Ferguson

Homeschooled in Memphis, Ferguson found fame as the nation’s youngest radio talk show host, going on the air at 13 and becoming nationally syndicated at 20. As his national celebrity grew, he left the Bluff City, and has expanded the audience for his rightwing podcasts and radio talk on such networks as Glenn Beck's Blaze.

61. Louise Fitzhugh (1928-1974)

Born and raised in Memphis (her family was wealthy, yet one summer she worked a job at The Commercial Appeal), Fitzhugh created a milestone of children's literature when she wrote and illustrated "Harriet the Spy," published in 1964 — "a superb portrait of an extraordinary child," per The New York Times. The book has remained in print ever since.

62. Ric Flair

"Regarded by multiple peers and journalists as the greatest professional wrestler of all time" (so says his Wikipedia entry), the Memphis-born 16-time world champion and self-described "Nature Boy" connects one of the city's key cultural commodities (wrestling) with one of its notorious scandals: Flair's adoption as a child was arranged by the agency run by the infamous Memphis baby trafficker, Georgia Tann.

63. Shelby Foote (1916-2005)

With a courtly Southern manner and drawl that captivated millions, this Memphis-based novelist and historian became an unlikely celebrity after he appeared in Ken Burns' hit PBS documentary series, "The Civil War," which drew inspiration in part from the three volumes of Foote's "The Civil War: A Narrative," published from 1958 to 1974.

64. Derek Fordjour

The son of Ghanian immigrants, the Memphis-born artist, who creates paintings, sculptures, collages and video projects, has had his work exhibited around the world and collected by such institutions as New York’s Whitney Museum.

65. Morgan Jon Fox

With "Blue Citrus Hearts," a same-sex coming-of-age romance, he emerged from the scrappy do-it-yourself digital scene of the early 2000s to be a generous mentor to other young filmmakers and a key contributor to numerous "indie" projects, while bringing national attention to the issue of "conversion therapy" with his 2011 activist documentary, "This Is What Love In Action Looks Like."

66. Aretha Franklin (1942-2018)

The "Queen of Soul" was born in 1942 at 406 Lucy in South Memphis, but lived here only about two months before her family moved north (waaay north) to Buffalo.

67. Morgan Freeman

Among the world’s most respected and in-demand actors, the sonorous star of “The Shawshank Redemption,” “Unforgiven,” “The Dark Knight” and many other memorable movies was born in Memphis but moved during infancy to Mississippi, where he continues to live and co-own the Ground Zero Blues Club.

68. Judy Freudberg (1949-2012)

An Emmy-winning longtime writer for "Sesame Street," this White Station High School graduate co-wrote the animated hits "An American Tail" and "The Land Before Time" for director Don Bluth and producer Steven Spielberg; but she may be more influential as a creator and writer for "Elmo's World," the "Sesame Street" segment that helped establish the ticklish red Muppet as an enduring children's icon.

69. John Fry (1944-2014)

A visionary mentor to generations of sonic innovators, this music-mad East Memphian founded Midtown’s Ardent Studios in the 1960s, attracting such simpatico clients over the decades as Big Star, the Replacements, Stevie Ray Vaughan and ZZ Top.

70. Jim Gaines (1941-2024)

This Memphis native learned his craft in local recording studios before moving to San Francisco and becoming one of the industry's most successful studio wizards, working as a sound engineer and producer on such popular albums as the Steve Miller Band's "Fly Like an Eagle," Van Morrison's "St. Dominic's Preview," George Thorogood's "Bad to the Bone," Huey Lewis' "Sports" and Santana's "Supernatural," which sold 30 million copies.

71. Gangsta Boo (1979-2023)

Whitehaven's Lola Chantrelle Mitchell began rapping with Three 6 Mafia as a teenager and soon was participating in million-selling records and collaborating with such artists as Eminem, Run the Jewels and Outkast. She died of an accidental overdose at 43.

72. The Gentrys

With two minutes of repetitious pop-rock perfection titled "Keep on Dancing," the Gentrys — a seven-member combo from Treadwell High School that included future wrestling star Jimmy Hart on vocals and lifelong rock-and-roller Larry Raspberry on guitar — scored a top 5 hit that sold more than a million copies in 1965.

73. GloRilla

With a platinum album ("Glorious") and a twice-platinum single ("TGIF") to her credit, this 26-year-old Frayser-raised hip-hop star (born Gloria Hallelujah Woods) is one of rap's great recent success stories, a sought-after collaborator who has recorded with Cardi B and toured with Megan Thee Stallion.

74. Ginnifer Goodwin

The St. Mary's Episcopal School graduate starred in HBO's polygamy drama "Big Love" and ABC's fairy tale-inspired "Once Upon a Time" but more recently has captivated children (of all ages) by providing the voice of officer Judy Hopps, a tireless bunny crusader, in Disney's animated "Zootopia" films.

75. Robert Gordon

The polymath author/moviemaker/historian and three-time Grammy winner has provided audiences with insight and entertainment for decades, via books, CD anthologies and documentaries that take deep dives into music, politics and culture. His new movie, "Newport & the Great Folk Dream," should hit theaters in 2027.

76. Rosco Gordon (1928-2002)

An associate of Johnny Ace, B.B. King, Bobby Bland and other so-called "Beale Streeters," this South Memphis bluesman was notable for a loping, syncopated piano style (as heard on such Memphis-made R&B hits as "Booted" and "No More Doggin'") that was a major influence on the development of ska and reggae music in Jamaica.

77. Yo Gotti

Born Mario Mims, the Memphis rapper and record executive has become a music-industry powerhouse, helping to launch the careers of such artists as GloRilla and Moneybagg Yo.

78. Clare Grant

A prolific Adult Swim voice actor but otherwise generally sexy screen presence, this former longtime Memphis resident specializes in science fiction, fantasy and horror spoofs proudly aimed at "geek" audiences and sometimes produced with her comedy ensemble, Team Unicorn, or with her husband, actor Seth Green.

79. Leonard Graves (1927-2000)

Understudy to the star, the Memphis-born singer and actor learned that it's good to be the king when he replaced Yul Brynner for multiple performances during the original Broadway run of the Rodgers-and-Hammerstein smash, "The King and I." But Graves was more familiar as a voice than as a face: He was the narrator of the epic 26-part NBC series "Victory at Sea," a World War II documentary that drew a huge audience during its original broadcast in 1952 and 1953.

80. Mark Greaney

The Memphis author with a degree in political science and international relations writes painstakingly researched espionage and action novels, including seven that continue Tom Clancy's "Jack Ryan" adventures and 15 in his own "Gray Man" series, the first of which was adapted into a Netflix movie with Ryan Gosling and Chris Evans.

81. Al Green

Arguably the greatest of all soul singers (or maybe the greatest of all singers, period), the swoon-inducing "Let's Stay Together" crooner scored eight gold-selling made-in-Memphis singles in the 1970s before making a (temporary) switch to gospel music.

82. The Grifters

The Memphis indie-rock postpunk quartet — Dave Shouse, Scott Taylor, Tripp Lamkins and Stan Gallimore — made waves in the 1990s, alongside such nationally renowned fellow travelers as Pavement and Guided by Voices.

83. John Grisham

Raised in Southaven and setting several of his books in Memphis, the world's best-selling author of legal thrillers — or of any type of books, just about — was for a time a one-man jobs generator for the Mid-South, with major-studio adaptations of "The Firm," "The Rainmaker" and "The Client" being filmed here in the 1990s, bringing such Hollywood folk to town as Susan Sarandon, Francis Ford Coppola and Tom Cruise.

84. Carl Gutherz (1844-1907)

With its gold-haloed angels and gauzy celestial sky, "Light of the Incarnation," from 1888, is typical of the many paintings in the collection of the Memphis Brooks Museum of Art by this Swiss-born and Paris-educated but largely Memphis-raised and Memphis-based artist, who contributed murals to the Library of Congress and was a source of local pride for those who preferred his idealized canvases to the unsettling innovations presented by some of his contemporaries.

85. Lucy Hale

Leaving Memphis for Los Angeles in her teens, Hale became a star as one of the five lead actors on "Pretty Little Liars," an ABC Family teen mystery that ran from 2010 to 2017.

86. Katori Hall

This Memphis-born-and-raised former intern with The Commercial Appeal achieved acclaim with her 2009 play "The Mountaintop," which cast Samuel L. Jackson as Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in its Broadway debut. She won the 2021 Pulitzer Prize for Drama for her Memphis-set "The Hot Wing King," and in 2020 she debuted her ongoing Starz network series,"P-Valley," set in a Mississippi Delta strip club.

87. Richard Halliburton (1900-1939)

Now forgotten by all but nostalgia buffs and the students who traverse the shadow of Richard Halliburton Memorial Tower on the Rhodes College campus, this Memphis best-selling travel writer and daring adventurer had his life of international celebrity cut short when he disappeared in 1939 while attempting to cross the Pacific Ocean in a Chinese junk. He was 39.

88. George Hamilton

The famously tan actor ("Love at First Bite") and gossip-page fixture (in 1966, he dated Lynda Bird Johnson, daughter of President LBJ) was born in Memphis (a "primrose-lined memory lane," he wrote in his autobiography) and lived for a time in the Parkview, at Overton Park.

89. W.C. Handy (1873-1958)

Immortalized with a statue on Beale Street, the "Father of the Blues" brought mainstream popularity and a level of respectability to America's authentic music with such compositions as "The Memphis Blues" (1912) and "Saint Louis Blues" (1914).

90. Chris Hardwick

The son of Billy Hardwick, the celebrity professional bowler, Chris Hardwick grew up in Memphis before relocating to California, where he became a Comedy Central regular, a game show MC, a pioneering podcaster and host of "Talking Dead," an hour-long "after show" discussion series that for 10 years followed AMC's zombie drama "The Walking Dead" and its spin-offs.

91. Roy Harrover (1928-2016)

The Yale-trained architect who put Memphis on the modernist map designed such signature spaces as Memphis International Airport, Mud Island River Park, the Church of the River and the Memphis College of Art in Overton Park (soon to be the new location of the Metal Museum).

92. Jimmy Hart

Hart first attracted attention as a member of the Gentrys (see above) but found greater fame and name recognition as the over-the-top professional wrestling manager nicknamed "The Mouth of the South."

93. Jon Hassell (1937-2021)

It's safe to say trumpeter Jon Hassell was the only member of the the Messick Class of 1955 high school band to become a giant of avant-garde composition, studying with the electronic music pioneer, Stockhausen, and the experimental minimalist, Terry Riley; contributing to the soundtrack of Martin Scorsese's "The Last Temptation of Christ"; and developing a "primitive/futuristic" sound that he called "Fourth World" music.

94. Isaac Hayes (1942-2008)

The prolific Stax songwriter became a global superstar with his sexy bald-pated "Black Moses" persona, his epically orchestrated arrangements of pop hits ("Walk On By") and his Oscar-winning "Theme from Shaft."

95. George Hearn

Active on the stage from his days as a student at Southwestern at Memphis, Hearn had flamboyant roles in some of musical theater’s biggest hits of recent decades: He was the lethal tonsorialist in “Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street” and the wizard in “Wicked"; and he won a Tony Award for his lead role as Albin in “La Cage Aux Folles” and for his supporting part as Max in “Sunset Boulevard," both of which roles he originated on Broadway.

96. Suzannah Herbert

The daughter of Memphis painter Pinkney Herbert has forged her own artistic identity as an acclaimed documentarian, most recently with “Natchez,” which examines the Mississippi tourist town’s problematic relationship with its antebellum identity.

97. Hi Rhythm Section

Guitarist Mabon “Teenie” Hodges, organist Charles Hodges, bassist Leroy Hodges, pianist Archie Turner and drummer Howard Grimes were the core members of this legendary ensemble, responsible for the funky yet otherworldly sound that backed up dozens of Hi hits by Al Green and his contemporaries at Willie Mitchell's Royal Studios.

98. Olivia Holt

Memphis, Germantown and DeSoto County were her home towns until the middle-school cheerleader moved to Southern California after being cast in the 2011-2015 Disney series "Kickin' It." Recently, she's become something of a Scream Queen, with roles in "Totally Killer" (slasher), "Heart Eyes" (serial killer) and "This Is Not a Test" (zombies).

99. The Hombres

Photographed in a garbage dump on the cover of their one and only album, this Memphis combo achieved garage rock immortality in 1967 with their drawling mindbender “Let It Out (Let It All Hang Out),” which opens with a Bronx cheer and the promise of “a preachment, dear friends… on John Barleycorn, nicotine, and the temptations of Eve."

100. John Lee Hooker (1917?-2001)

The future blues legend began his career on Beale Street after he moved from Mississippi to Memphis in the 1930s, but he did not hit it big with such songs as “Boogie Chillen” until he relocated to Detroit.

101. Howlin' Wolf (1910-1976)

The most formidable of postwar bluesmen ("I'm 300 pounds of muscle and man," he sang), the former Chester Arthur Burnett cut such classics as "Moanin' at Midnight" at Sun before finding greater success at Chess Records in Chicago.

102. Alberta Hunter (1895-1984)

Raised in a Memphis bordello, Hunter began making records in the 1920s, then experienced a career revival in the 1970s.

103. Jason Isbell

Like his fellow future Drive-By Truckers members, Patterson Hood and Mike Cooley (whose early band, Adam’s House Cat, was based here briefly in the 1990s), Isbell spent formative musical years in Memphis, writing songs and playing in such venues as the Map Room while pursuing an English degree at the University of Memphis.

104. Al Jackson Jr. (1935-1975)

Dubbed “The Human Timekeeper,” the Booker T. & the MG’s drummer was shot to death at home in 1975. His murder remains unsolved.

105. George Jackson (1945-2013)

While cutting his own records for numerous Memphis labels, Jackson wrote hundreds of songs, including hits for the Osmonds (“One Bad Apple”) and Bob Seger (“Old Time Rock and Roll”).

106. Cordell Jackson (1923-2004)

A pioneering 1950s woman record producer and label owner (Moon Records was her answer to Sun), Jackson in later years emerged as a guitar-thrashing "Rock 'n' Roll Granny" and role model/mentor to a new generation of do-it-yourself punks.

107. Jimi Jamison (1951-2014)

The Memphis hard rock vocalist fronted Target, Cobra and Survivor, and co-wrote and performed “I’m Always Here,” the theme song for the TV series “Baywatch.”

108. Roland Janes (1933-2013)

The ex-Sun guitarist operated his aptly named Sonic Recording Service in Memphis from 1963 until 1974, overseeing fearlessly inventive tracks by such guitar gunslingers as Travis Wammack.

109. Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson

Before becoming an eyebrow-arching Hollywood superstar and even before anyone could smell what The Rock was cookin', Johnson followed in his father Rocky Johnson’s lace-booted footsteps as a professional wrestler in the 1990s on the wild-and-woolly Memphis circuit, an era he chronicled in the set-in-Memphis and shot-in-Memphis episodes of his autobiographical NBC television series, “Young Rock."

110. Booker T. Jones

Master of the Hammond B-3 organ, the elegant namesake of the Stax house band, Booker T. & the MG’s, is a Grammy Lifetime Achievement recipient.

111. Busta Jones (1951-1995)

He toured with bluesman Albert King but the Memphis bass player born Michael Jones was best known for his funky contributions to the recordings and stage shows of such artsy and adventurous rock musicians as Brian Eno, Gang of Four and Talking Heads.

112. Leslie Jones

The 6-foot Memphis-born former “Saturday Night Live” cast member and “Ghostbusters" (2016) star has been a boisterous, larger-than-life comedy presence for the past 30 years.

113. Juicy J

Emerging from the lo-fi "horrorcore" hip-hop underground, this Three 6 Mafia co-founder (birth name: Jordan Houston) helped propel Memphis and Southern rap into the mainstream, selling millions of records and earning a Best Original Song Oscar.

114. Valerie June

Based in Memphis while she developed her idiosyncratic old-timey yet progressive style, the Jackson, Tennessee-born singer-songwriter has become a star in recent years, mesmerizing audiences with what she calls her "organic moonshine roots music" — and with her voluminous coils of dreadlocks.

115. Florence Kahn (1878-1951)

A product of Memphis' finishing and private schools, Kahn was a fixture in artistic and prestigious stage productions in late 19th-century and early 20th-century New York, appearing opposite the most acclaimed stars of the day, such as Richard Mansfield, in works by Shakespeare, Ibsen and Maeterlinck.

116. Al Kapone

Born Aphonzo Jerome Bailey, the South Memphis hip-hop veteran who often punches up his "crunk" street sound with horns and other elements of classic R&B will forever be beloved (and blamed) for "Whoop That Trick," the riotous rap anthem that became ubiquitous after it migrated from the soundtrack of "Hustle & Flow" to Memphis' nightclubs and sports arenas.

117. Gere Kavanaugh

A postwar pioneer touted as one of General Motors' "Damsels of Design" (as the company called its woman artists), the Memphis Academy of Arts graduate has designed fabrics, furniture, kitchenware, umbrellas, typeface and much, much more.

118. Stan Kesler (1928-2020)

The busy musician/engineer/producer/songwriter participated in the creation of innumerable Memphis masterpieces, from Elvis' Sun sessions (he wrote "I Forgot to Remember to Forget") to Sam the Sham's novelty rock (he produced "Wooly Bully").

119. Albert King (1923-1992)

Born in Indianola and "Born Under a Bad Sign," King — accompanied by his signature Gibson Flying V guitar — was the biggest blues star on the Stax roster.

120. B.B. King (1925-2015)

The "Beale Street Blues Boy" was a fixture in local clubs and a disc jockey on WDIA radio until his undeniable talent and tireless touring schedule enabled him to become the world-renowned "King of the Blues."

121. Walter Lang (1896-1972)

Described by The Commercial Appeal in 1938 as "the crack 20th Century Fox director who still likes to call Memphis his home," the Memphis-born Lang was perhaps the most successful filmmaker ever to emerge from the Bluff City, helming more than 60 features from the silent era through the 1960s, working with such stars as Shirley Temple, Marilyn Monroe and Katharine Hepburn, and earning a Best Director nomination for the Oscar-anointed Best Picture of 1956, "The King and I." His final film was "Snow White and the Three Stooges," in 1961.

122. Snooky Lanson (1914-1990)

A big band “boy singer” in the 1930s, Lanson succeeded Frank Sinatra as a regular vocalist on the NBC series “Your Hit Parade,” from 1950 to 1957.

123. Jerry Lawler

Inspired by his lifelong love for the costumed brawlers who occupy wrestling rings and comic books, "The King" has been a dominant force in professional wrestling for half a century, bringing national attention to Memphis through his feud with performance artist/comedian Andy Kaufman, and commanding the spotlight as a wrestler and announcer with the WWE.

124. Arthur Lee (1945-2006)

Leaving Memphis for Los Angeles before he was a teenager, Lee led the psychedelic rock band Love, whose album “Forever Changes” is regarded as a Summer of Love masterpiece.

125. Adriane Lenox

Active in Memphis church and school productions since childhood, Lenox won a Tony Award in 2005 for her performance in John Patrick Shanley's "Doubt"; but she is probably most familiar as the drug-addict mother of high school football star Michael Oher (Quinton Aaron) in the 2009 movie "The Blind Side."

126. Furry Lewis (1899?-1981)

A one-legged City of Memphis street sweeper, Lewis cut records in the 1920s, then returned to performing in the 1950s. He acted opposite Burt Reynolds in a 1975 movie ("W.W. and the Dixie Dancekings"), opened for the Rolling Stones at the Liberty Bowl in 1976, and was immortalized in song ("Furry Sings the Blues") by Joni Mitchell in 1976.

127. Jerry Lee Lewis (1935-2022)

Whether pounding his piano to "Great Balls of Fire" or marrying his 13-year-old cousin, the Sun Records "Killer" spurned convention to embrace the paradoxically Pentecostal-influenced hellfire abandon of rock 'n' roll.

128. Alan Lightman

A physicist and prolific essayist now in the Department of Humanities at MIT, his 1992 novel “Einstein’s Dream,” which examines the science and philosophy of time, was an international best-seller.

129. Lil Buck

Whether dancing with Madonna during the Super Bowl halftime show, appearing in a Spike Lee film or touring with Cirque du Soleil, Charles "Lil Buck" Riley has been the world's most celebrated exemplar of "jookin," a sinuous yet also sometimes jerky style of Memphis street dance that delights audiences at all levels of class and culture.

130. Booker Little (1938-1961)

Another musical prodigy from Manassas High School, Little played trumpet with John Coltrane and Max Roach and seemed destined to be a Memphis jazz superstar until he died at 23 of apparent kidney damage.

131. Charles Lloyd

A philosopher and master of reed instruments, his 1966 album “Forest Flower: Charles Lloyd at Monterey” was one of the first jazz albums to sell more than a million copies.

132. Babbie Lovett

A fixture of newspaper society pages back when Memphis was a fashion hub of the South, this self-described "wild child" (now a nonagenarian) is a rare Memphis fashion celebrity — a buyer, collector, promoter, innovator, muse and model for such designers as Calvin Klein, Bill Blass, Oleg Cassini and Halston.

133. Lucero

Fronted by Ben Nichols, the Memphis alt-country-rock band — members include such local warriors of the rock 'n' roll trenches as John Stubblefield, Brian Venable, Roy Berry and Rick Steff — has issued some 20 albums since 2000.

134. Jimmie Lunceford (1902-1947)

The first public high school band director in Memphis, this former gym teacher transformed his Manassas High group, the Chickasaw Syncopators, into a professional "hot jazz" ensemble that toured the country and rivaled the popularity of the Duke Ellington and Cab Calloway orchestras.

135. Harold Mabern (1936-2019)

“A Few Miles from Memphis” (1968) is among the albums recorded by this soulful post-bop pianist.

136. Terry Manning (1947-2025)

A quarterback at Central High, Manning also was a trusted playmaker at Stax and Ardent, engineering and producing records by Big Star, Led Zeppelin and the Staple Singers.

137. Wink Martindale (1933-2025)

The Memphis radio and kiddie show personality (he dressed in a sort of Buck Rogers outfit for WHBQ's "Mars Patrol") enjoyed a long career as a personable and clean-cut national game show host, highlighted by a seven-year run on the syndicated "Tic-Tac-Dough."

138. Mike McCarthy

For more than 30 years this Elvis- and Bowie-obsessed comic book artist, sculptor, musician and writer-director has championed "unpopular culture" through drive-in screenings, punk rock burlesque shows, and his own shoestring-budget cult films-in-search-of-a-cult (i.e., "Damselvis, Daughter of Helvis").

139. Hilton McConnico (1943-2018)

This self-taught designer who attended Central High School created gowns for Memphis Cotton Carnival queens before leaving for Paris in 1965 and becoming globally recognized for his clothes, crystal products, restaurants and even movie sets: He was production designer on the famously stylish 1981 French cult classic, "Diva."

140. The Memphis Boys

Featuring guitarist Reggie Young, drummer Gene Chrisman, pianist Bobby Wood, organist Bobby Emmons and bassists Mike Leech and Tommy Cogbill, this legendary session band from 1967 to 1972 reputedly cut more than 120 chart records — an unmatched achievement — at its home base, Chips Moman's American Sound Studio.

141. The Memphis Horns

Trumpeter Wayne Jackson (1941-2016) and saxophonist Andrew Love (1941-2012) played on dozens of gold and platinum albums by Otis Redding, Peter Gabriel, U2 and others.

142. Memphis Minnie (1897-1973)

Famously reworked by Led Zeppelin, "When the Levee Breaks," from 1929, was among the notable songs recorded by the former Lizzie Douglas, who began singing for change on Beale Street while a teenager.

143. Memphis Slim (1915-1988)

Born John Len Chatman, the prolific piano-playing blues vocalist and composer cut hundreds of records for multiple labels but found greater appreciation as well as steadier remuneration after he moved to Paris, France, in 1962.

144. John Jackson Miller

Comic books and best-selling novels multiply like tribbles from the pen (or computer) of this extraordinarily prolific Memphis born-and-raised writer, who has carved out a successful career contributing to the “Star Wars,” “Star Trek” and Batman bookshelves.

145. Ronnie Milsap

Moving to Memphis in the late 1960s, the North Carolina-born Milsap played on Elvis' "Kentucky Rain" and other hits before he relocated to Nashville to become a top country artist.

146. Willie Mitchell (1928-2010)

A bandleader, trumpeter, songwriter and producer, Mitchell was an architect of the immediately identifiable yet inimitable Hi Records sound that fueled some of the greatest popular music ever created: the songs that Al Green, Ann Peebles and others cut at Royal Studios on South Lauderdale in the 1970s, with backing from the tight but expressive Hi Rhythm Section.

147. Chips Moman (1937-2016)

His American Sound Studio at 827 Thomas St. helped make Memphis a national center of the recording industry by churning out dozens of hit records in the 1960s and 1970s, including Elvis' "Suspicious Minds," Neil Diamond's "Sweet Caroline" and Dusty Springfield's "Son of a Preacher Man."

148. Moneybagg Yo

A product of South Memphis and Mitchell High School, Moneybagg Yo has been manifesting the profitable promise of his professional name for almost a decade, with his fourth studio album, “A Gangsta’s Pain,” topping the Billboard charts in 2021.

149. Sputnik Monroe (1928-2006)

A flamboyant professional grappler with a barrel chest, a motor mouth, a practiced scowl and a blond skunk stripe racing through his hair to match the gleaming championship belt circumnavigating his waist, Sputnik was a heel in the ring and a hero for real: In his heyday in the late 1950s, the white professional wrestling superstar made headlines for defying city segregation laws. He insisted that Black fans be allowed to sit in seats that had been designated "whites only," and he went to court to battle a disorderly conduct charge, after being arrested for what an officer described as the "crime" of "drinking in a negro cafe with negros."

150. Scotty Moore (1931-2016)

The guitarist for Elvis Presley’s Sun sessions, Moore’s 1964 solo album was aptly titled “The Guitar That Changed the World.”

151. Charlie Musselwhite

Sleepy-eyed and effortlessly cool, the harmonica-playing Robert Mitchum of the blues (he even ran moonshine, like Mitchum in "Thunder Road") immersed himself in Memphis music as a youth before heading to Chicago and then California, where "Memphis Charlie," as he was known, became a preeminent "white bluesman."

152. Zach Myers

Touring professionally by age 14, the Memphis guitarist joined the Florida-founded hard rock band Shinedown in 2005, in his early 20s.

153. Elise Neal

The actress, dancer and Overton High School alum was cast as a member of the title family in the ABC/UPN sitcom “The Hughleys” and has appeared in movies directed by Spike Lee, John Singleton and Craig Brewer.

154. Hal Needham (1931-2013)

The Memphis-born stuntman turned moviemaker directed "Smokey and the Bandit," the No. 2 box office hit of 1977, behind "Star Wars."

155. Phineas Newborn Jr. (1931-1989)

Described by The New York Times as "one of the three greatest jazz pianists of all time," Newborn — who learned his trade playing in Memphis blues and jazz bands, often with his brother, guitarist Calvin Newborn — was plagued by poor health but nevertheless recorded a series of albums now regarded as masterpieces, such as "A World of Piano!" (1962).

156. Ollie Nightingale (1936-1997)

The lead singer of the Dixie Nightingales, a Memphis-based gospel group, the former Ollie Hoskins pursued secular success with his vocal group, Ollie & the Nightingales, but earned more airplay (and raised more eyebrows) as a solo artist with his 1999 "grown folk" blues hit, "I'll Drink Your Bathwater, Baby."

157. Don Nix (1941-2024)

A saxophonist in the original Stax house band, the Mar-Keys, Nix — the writer of the rock standard, “Going Down” — was a Zelig-like rock ‘n' roll presence, bringing his musical acumen and handlebar mustache to sessions by Leon Russell and Jeff Beck and to such events as George Harrison’s Concert for Bangladesh.

158. NLE Choppa

Released when he was 17, this Parkway Village rapper's 2019 single "Shotta Flow" sold 3 million copies, in its original and remixed versions.
